# Attackers use Hugging Face’s AI to make phishing pages

## TL;DR

- Hugging Face Spaces are git repositories that Hugging Face hosts and serves as apps. DeepSite, Hugging Face's AI website builder, generates a site from a prompt and publishes it as a Space. Each Space gets its own *.hf.space URL that anyone can open, that's how phishing pages are hosted.

- On October 16, 2026, we found 42 phishing and credential-stealing pages on Hugging Face Spaces. They impersonated 28 brands, including Microsoft, Google, PayPal, Chase, and Coinbase.

- We reported all 42 pages to Hugging Face the same day. By October 29, all of them were paused or no longer publicly reachable.

- 29 of the pages were built with DeepSite, Hugging Face’s AI website builder. One Microsoft login clone took about 90 minutes of plain-language prompts, and other operators asked the builder to hide their pages from crawlers or send stolen logins to Telegram.

- What to do: check your DNS, Firewall, and email gateway logs for the phishing hostnames at the end of this post, if present, reset the associated users’ passwords, applicable credentials, and review logs for unauthorized activity, lastly treat hf.space links in email like any other free hosting domain.

- Aikido Noon catches phishing links like these hosted from Hugging Face pages, through link detonation and screenshot analysis, even on trusted hosts like Hugging Face.

Hugging Face is best known for AI models, but anyone can also publish a web page or app there, called a Space, at its own address on hf.space. If your company uses Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or any of the brands listed below, phishing emails your staff have received may link to pages hosted on Hugging Face. Search your proxy, DNS and email gateway logs for the hostnames in the indicators of compromise. For any match, reset the user's password, sign them out of all active sessions, and review sign-in activity since the visit, because many of these pages also captured one-time codes. More below.

First we'll cover who's affected and what to do, then how one Jupyter notebook led us to 42 phishing pages and why attackers host them on Hugging Face. After that we get into the analysis: what the pages impersonated, how two-thirds were built by prompting DeepSite, and how long they stayed up. We’ll finish with disclosure, takeaways, how Aikido detects this kind of phishing, and the full list of indicators of compromise.

Aikido Noon catches phishing on fake websites through link detonation and screenshot analysis, even on trusted hosts like Hugging Face.

## Who’s affected

Anyone whose employees or customers got a phishing email linking to one of these pages. They targeted:

- Work email and identity: Microsoft 365, Google and Gmail, Roundcube, Zimbra, Orange Mail and ID.me

- Banks and payments: PayPal, Bank of America, Chase, Coinbase, Scotiabank, CIBC, Coris Bank, Orange Money and SumUp

- Social and gaming accounts: Instagram, Facebook, Netflix, Discord, Adobe, Roblox, Brawl Stars and Growtopia

## Who isn’t

If you only use Hugging Face to download models or datasets, this doesn’t affect your code. These were standalone web pages hosted on HF spaces, not models, datasets or packages.

## What to do

- Check your logs. Search proxy, DNS and email gateway logs for the hostnames in the indicators table at the end of this post.

- If you get a match, treat the account as compromised. Reset the password, sign the user out of all active sessions, and review sign-in activity since the visit. Many of these pages also captured one-time codes, so two-factor authentication alone doesn’t mean the account is safe. If card or bank details were entered, contact the bank.

- Look closely at hf.space links in email. Flag inbound emails that link to hf.space.

- Tell your team. A login page on a trusted platform isn’t proof the page is real. Microsoft, Google or your bank will never ask you to sign in on hf.space.

- Report anything new to Hugging Face at security@huggingface.co.

## How it started

Our discovery started with one repo. Aikido’s malware scanning flagged agentamrorg/AIAMR-model-a-pub, a Jupyter notebook on Hugging Face whose markdown cell hides a <script> that draws a fake Hugging Face login. The repo turned out to be a self-labeled security test, but this got us asking, “who else is hosting phishing pages on Hugging Face?”

We pointed an AI agent at that one sample and asked it to find more like it. In one afternoon, we found 42 phishing and credential-stealing pages. With AI, we’re able to find phishing pages that stayed online for more than a year in just one afternoon.

One of them, cgfcbftdsf/microsoft-auth-portal, is a fake Microsoft login page served from cgfcbftdsf-microsoft-auth-portal.static.hf.space. It sends the victim’s email, password, phone number and date of birth to a Telegram bot, then redirects them to the real Outlook. Hugging Face tagged it deepsite-v3, which means it was built with DeepSite, Hugging Face’s AI website builder. You describe the page you want in plain language, DeepSite writes the HTML, CSS and JavaScript using an open-weight model, and the result is published as a Space.

It isn’t uncommon. Two-thirds of the 42 pages we discovered were built with DeepSite, and more than half had been online for over a year.

## Why do attackers phish on Hugging Face?

The domain is trusted. A page on hf.space gets HTTPS and an established domain tied to a platform developers trust. It skips the warning signs filters look for in a newly registered lookalike domain, and blocking *.hf.space outright would also block every legitimate demo hosted there.

Hosting is free and instant. A static Space is plain HTML/JS with no server or hosting bill behind it, and it goes live the moment it’s pushed.

The platform builds it for you. DeepSite turns a description into a page and publishes it straight to a Space. You don’t need a phishing kit, or the skills to write one.

## How we found the pages

From the initial Jupyter notebook, we searched Hugging Face for pages that send data to: Telegram bots, Discord webhooks or form services, and for repos named after brands. These pages are static, so wherever they send stolen credentials has to be written into the page itself. We flagged every page with a login form that sent data to one of those places, then checked each one by hand to rule out real sites and empty templates.

### Limitation of our search

Our search only found pages that send data to the chat apps and form services, so pages using other exfiltration methods won’t appear here. We also didn’t see visitor data, so we can’t say how many people visited these pages or entered credentials.

## What we found

When we found the pages on October 16, 34 of the 42 pages were live and 8 were paused. Most sent stolen data to a Telegram bot (25 of them). Eleven used a Discord webhook and six used a form service. The pages asked for more than passwords: one-time codes, full card details, bank transaction passwords, phone numbers and dates of birth. Many also logged the victim’s IP address, then sent the user on to the real site so nothing looked wrong.

## Two-thirds were built with AI

So how do we know these were built with Hugging Face’s DeepSite? DeepSite leaves fingerprints on the pages it builds, and 29 of the 42 pages we found have them:

- The tag. Every page DeepSite publishes gets a deepsite or deepsite-v3 tag. All 29 have it.

- The badge. 26 of the 29 link back to Hugging Face’s DeepSite ( enzostvs-deepsite.hf.space , huggingface.co/deepsite or deepsite.hf.co ), either through the “Made with DeepSite” badge on the page or in the README.

- The README. A lot of them still have DeepSite’s default text: “Welcome to your new DeepSite project! This project was created with DeepSite.”

- The commit history. When you ask DeepSite to change something, it saves your request as a commit. In 24 of the 29 pages, the commit messages are exactly that, the attacker’s instructions to the builder.

The commit history of the Microsoft phishing page from the intro, cgfcbftdsf/microsoft-auth-portal, shows what that process looks like. It was built in 15 commits, 14 of them within 90 minutes on October 25, 2025. Every commit after the first is an instruction to the builder, written in French.

The Microsoft page wasn't the only one built this way. Across the DeepSite pages, operators were open with the site builder about what they wanted. Two prompts asked, in Hindi and English, to build an “Instagram verified phishing page.” Others asked the builder to send everything entered on the page to a Telegram bot, to forward logins “along with the user agent and IP” before redirecting the victim to their own email provider, or simply: “button does not send to discord webhook, fix it”.

Some went further. One prompt asked the site builder to check the visitor’s user agent and hide the page from Googlebot, Bingbot, headless browsers, curl and wget, which is filtering that keeps a page away from security scanners. Another asked it to reject the first password attempt with “incorrect credentials, please try again,” so the victim types it twice. Across the sites the prompts were written in French, English, Hindi, Portuguese, Indonesian and Russian.

The 13 pages without the DeepSite tag all came from three repeat operators: Account-sign-in, which ran eight brand pages from a single account, plus asigmaguy and ntrsdasda. These operators appear to bring their own kits. The DeepSite pages were mostly one-offs, prompted into existence by people who may never have written a phishing kit by hand.

## Online for more than a year

The oldest page, InstagramPage/look-this, went up on April 26, 2025, almost 18 months before we found it.

The three newest were all from asigmaguy, published in late July and early August 2026. 39 of the 42 hadn’t been updated in six months or more. These are publish dates from git history: they show how long each page existed, but can’t show how long it was actually serving.

## Disclosure

We reported all 42 pages to Hugging Face on October 16, the day we found them. Hugging Face acted on the report, and by October 29 every one of them was paused or removed. None are serving victims today. We thank HuggingFace for taking this seriously.

## What to take from this

Building a phishing page used to take a kit, some HTML and somewhere to host it. The Microsoft login clone in this post took about 90 minutes of plain-language instructions to an AI builder, and Hugging Face hosted the result for free. Two-thirds of the pages we found were made the same way using Hugging Face’s resources.

Any platform that lets AI build and publish pages without restriction is bound to end up hosting phishing. Hugging Face is just where we looked. The builder was told to copy Microsoft’s official logo and the official Outlook login background, and it did, with no pushback. Once these pages were published, more than half stayed up for over a year.

Here’s what could change. A static page that collects credentials and posts them to a Telegram bot or Discord webhook is easy to spot without running it, on any domain. Platforms that host AI-built pages could check for that pattern at publish time. In the meantime, treat *.hf.space like any other free hosting domain.
